title: the Rudram
hook: the Rudram looks up at the sun crossing the sky, copper and red, and says the cowherds have seen him

segments.voice: Yesterday the Rudram opened with a bow to anger and asked Rudra to unstring the bow. Whose anger did you name before you answered it? Day one thousand one hundred forty-seven.

Early morning in a village. A boy is driving cattle out to graze. A woman walks back from the well with a water pot on her hip. Neither of them is a priest. Neither is chanting anything. And the sun is coming up over the fields, copper, then red, then a warm brown glow. Still in its opening section, the Rudram turns and points at that sun. That one, it says. The cowherds have seen him. The women carrying water have seen him. Today: where this hymn says Rudra can be seen.
screen: `A BOY WITH CATTLE.` → `A WOMAN WITH A WATER POT.` → `THE SUN COMING UP.`

segments.voice: The verses describe a figure in the sky. That one who is copper-colored, and red, and brown, and wholly auspicious. Around him, the hymn says, are more Rudras, on every side, and it asks that their anger be turned aside. Then it describes him moving across the sky, the one with the blue throat, glowing red. And then the surprising line. The cowherds have seen him. The water-carrying women have seen him. All beings have seen him. And may he, seen, be kind to us. Some readers, following the old commentary, take this figure as the sun, rising and crossing the sky. On that reading, Rudra is not hidden in a cave or locked in a temple. He's up there in plain view, every morning. And the people named as having seen him aren't sages or kings. They're a cowherd and a woman fetching water. Ordinary people in the village, doing ordinary work. That's the move. The fierce god of yesterday's opening, the archer with his bow drawn, is also the light that falls on everyone's morning chores. On the hymn's terms, no special training is needed to see him. Only looking up. And the hymn adds that small phrase: seen. May he, having been seen, be kind. As if seeing him is itself part of the relationship. The blue throat is worth a note too. We met it in the sahasranama, with the churning of the ocean. The Rudram doesn't tell that story. It just calls him the blue-throated one, and moves on.
screen: `COPPER, RED, BROWN — AUSPICIOUS.` · `THE BLUE-THROATED ONE, GLOWING.` · `THE COWHERDS HAVE SEEN HIM.` · `SEEN, MAY HE BE KIND.` · then, large: `ONLY LOOKING UP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let the light be seen. Sit where there's some light, from a window, a lamp, even a screen turned away. Let your eyes rest near it without staring. Notice its color. Warm or cool, bright or dim. Notice where it falls: on your hands, on the floor. Remember the cowherd and the woman with the water pot, who saw what the hymn saw without stopping their work. If you pray, you can greet the light as the hymn does, as Rudra, as Shiva. The bell holds the time.
The Rudram. Today's passage: the copper-red one crossing the sky, seen by the cowherds and the women carrying water.
Your line: the Rudram. Today, look at the sky once on purpose, during an ordinary errand, the way a cowherd might. Day one thousand one hundred forty-seven.

howItsDone: The Rudram is chanted in Sanskrit, in a fixed Vedic intonation passed from teacher to student; some Hindus chant it at dawn, and the sun appears in its opening section as a form of Rudra.

fork.setup: you're writing a hymn to a fierce god. you want to name who has seen him. who does the Rudram name?
fork.reveal: the hymn names a cowherd and a woman fetching water: ordinary people doing ordinary work, who see him in the morning sky.

what it means: Rudra crosses the sky as the copper-red sun, seen by cowherds and women carrying water.
what a scholar hears: Taittiriya Samhita 4.5.1, the asau yas tamro aruna verses: the sun as Rudra, nilagriva vilohita, seen by gopa and udaharyah.

notes: Paraphrased from memory of the first anuvaka: asau yas tamro aruna uta babhruh sumangalah ... ye cemam rudra abhito dikshu shritah sahasrasho; asau yo 'vasarpati nilagrivo vilohitah, utainam gopa adrishan adrishann udaharyah, utainam vishva bhutani, sa drishto mridayati nah.
